newsitem.title: USA: USDA 96/97 world coffee forecast likely lower.
newsitem.headline: USDA 96/97 world coffee forecast likely lower.

text.p: Two months after the U.S. Department of Agriculture issued its 1996/97 world coffee production estimate, a USDA analyst said a revision for global output would probably come in lower than its last forecast in December.
"Based on widely available news reports from the past two months, I would guess the next revision is more likely to be down than up," said Edmond Missiaen, a speciality crops analyst at the USDA.

In December, the USDA estimated 1996/97 global coffee output at 100.9 million 60-kg bags, with the recovery of the Brazilian crop after two severe frost accounting for all the 10-million-bag increase from the previous season.
Missiaen declined to forecast any downward revision and the USDA is not scheduled to release another world production estimate until June 12.
However, Missiaen reiterated the December findings that a more than six percent increase in world coffee exports during the 1996/97 season should enable consuming countries to build stockpiles.

"World coffee exports in 1996/97 are forecast at 79.6 million bags, up more than five million bags from estimated 1995/96 exports," he said. "If realized, exports at this level will allow some rebuilding of depleted stocks in importing countries."

Missiaen said the world coffee supply would hinge on the output from top-grower Brazil. Brazil, which produced about a quarter of the world's coffee in the last five seasons, marks the difference between a surplus and a deficit in global coffee supplies.

Frosts in 1994/95 reduced Brazil's 1995/96 crop to 16.8 million bags, but crop recovery due to good weather and better plantation management resulted in a 1996/97 yield of some 27 million bags, he said.

While the frosts were still likely to impact the outlook for the 1997/98 Brazilian harvest, Missiaen said the crop size would be determined by the weather, which he added has been favorable so far, the continued recovery from frost damage, expectations of an "off" year in the two-year production cycle and plantation care.
He noted that excellent plantation care should help to offset the "off" year phenomenon, which he estimated could result in a decrease of up to four million bags of coffee.

Although the USDA has made no preliminary estimate for the Brazil 1997/98 crop, Missiaen said by taking into account the previous season's 27 million bag estimate, a zero to four million bag decrease due to the "off" year cycle and an increase of at least one million bags coming from the recovery crop would point to a 1997/98 harvest between 24 and 28 million bags.
He stressed, however, that this was not a USDA estimate. "It is just a forecast based on me sitting at my desk in Washington D.C.," Missiaen said.

Preliminary estimates by industry sources in Brazil have ranged from 18 million to 23 million bags for the 1997/98 coffee crop. But talk emerged Friday that ex-USDA representative and private forecaster Leon Yallouz had put the crop at 27.5 million bags.

In Central America, Missiaen said producing nations should yield "decent" crops, although there were some reports of damage from heavy rains last year. He noted, however, that Central America experienced a similar phenomena to Colombia, where higher price incentives have led to better plantation care.

The USDA estimated in December that second-leading producer Colombia would harvest 12.5 million bags in 1996/97. But less than two weeks ago, a Colombia National Coffee Growers' official said there would be a "drastic drop" in the country's output during the current coffee year.
Revising previous estimates of Colombia's production, John Naranjo said output could drop as low as 10.4 million bags, from 12.9 million bags in 1995/96.
